orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the order entered on or about February 25, 2020.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted dismissal against the two moving defendants.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff alleged a slip on snow or ice on or near the supermarket parking driveway. Defendants’ meteorologist reported no measurable event for 19 days, no accumulation in exposed undisturbed areas for 11 days, and no ice/snow at the location for at least 85 hours.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff’s theory of melting/refreezing from improperly removed snow was speculative and refuted by climatological records; no negligent removal found.

Weather evidence negated snow/ice at the location during the relevant period; plaintiff’s alternative accumulation theories raised no factual issue. This is not an inability-to-identify testimony ruling.
Defendants’ meteorologist and climatological data established entitlement to dismissal; plaintiff’s accumulation/melt-refreeze theories were speculative and refuted by the records.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants’ meteorologist interpreted the climatological data; report format unspecified.
Climatological records supported the no-accumulation intervals and refuted the opposing theories.

quality.notes: Review boundary: on or near the parking driveway does not place the actual fall on private premises. Driveway vicinity is other location, not necessarily parking lot. Preserve alleged snow/ice despite contrary weather evidence. No storm-in-progress holding; no accident date or customer role inferred. Unchanged rules for 2021 opinion.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Wilma Guzman, J.), entered on or about February 25, 2020, which granted defendants 100-120 Hugh Grant Circle Realty, LLC and JSMD Food Corp.'s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against them, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Plaintiff alleged that he sustained personal injuries when he slipped and fell as a result of snow/ice on or near the parking driveway of defendants' supermarket.

Defendants established their prima facie entitlement to summary judgment through their expert meteorologist, who concluded that climatological data showed that the last measurable weather event was 19 days prior to plaintiff's accident, there was no snow or ice present in undisturbed, untreated, exposed areas for at least 11 days prior to plaintiff's accident, and ice and snow would not have been present at the location for at least 85 hours prior to the accident

In opposition, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. His argument that snow and ice might have accumulated from earlier storms, or from melting and refreezing snow not properly removed by defendants, was speculative and refuted by the climatological records

orders.description: Defendant’s limited appeal from the April 5, 2018 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of the amended complaint against Pyramid.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on about five inches of snow in the owned/operated shopping-mall parking lot around 2:30 p.m. She testified it was snowing; her husband said snowfall stopped during the preceding two hours while they shopped.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant’s submissions did not establish that an ongoing storm caused the injuries: accounts conflicted and expert/data did not show snowfall after 12:54 p.m. at the location.
Meteorologist’s affidavit and supporting data were insufficient to establish snow after 12:54 p.m.; no definitive storm-end time was found.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described snowfall at 2:30 p.m. and about five inches on the lot.
Husband testified it stopped snowing during the preceding shopping period.
Defendant submitted a meteorologist affidavit, insufficient on storm timing.
Data relied on by meteorologist did not establish snowfall after 12:54 p.m.; specific data format unstated.

quality.notes: Express mall ownership supports private lot. Shopping supports customer role. Conflicting timing defeats initial burden without proving no storm or fixing cessation. No actual accident date or notice finding supplied.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Plaintiff commenced this action seeking to recover damages for injuries that she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on snow in the parking lot of a shopping mall owned and operated by Pyramid Walden Company, L.P.

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Genesee County (Emilio L. Colaiacovo, J.), entered April 5, 2018. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the motion of defendant Pyramid Walden Company, L.P., for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint against it.

Supreme Court properly denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that there was a storm in progress inasmuch as defendant failed to meet its prima facie burden of establishing that plaintiff's injuries were caused by a storm in progress

Defendant submitted the deposition testimony of plaintiff, who testified that it was snowing at approximately 2:30 p.m. when she slipped and fell on approximately five inches of snow in the parking lot. Defendant, however, also submitted the testimony of plaintiff's husband, who testified that it stopped snowing sometime during the preceding two-hour period, while he and plaintiff were shopping.
The affidavit of defendant's expert meteorologist and the data upon which he relied were insufficient to establish that it was snowing after 12:54 p.m. at the location of the accident

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the May 13, 2020 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over a cart stacked with empty boxes in a store aisle. In her opposition affidavit she acknowledged seeing the cart on entering the aisle but forgetting it was there when she tripped.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the rule eliminating protection/warning duty for a condition both obvious and not inherently dangerous.
Cart was readily observable, known to plaintiff and not inherently dangerous. Forgetting it did not make it a trap for the unwary; no triable issue raised.
Plaintiff provided no evidentiary basis that further discovery would yield relevant evidence or essential facts exclusively controlled by defendant; summary judgment was not premature.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s opposition affidavit acknowledged prior observation of the cart.

quality.notes: Store interior supports private control; no ownership, customer status, date or creation/notice finding inferred. No separate assumption-of-risk/comparative-fault holding. Discovery argument is ancillary to merits. Unchanged rules for 2022 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she alleged she sustained when she tripped and fell over a cart stacked with empty boxes in an aisle of the defendant's store.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Joseph Farneti, J.), dated May 13, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
In an affidavit submitted in opposition to the motion the plaintiff stated that she observed the cart when she entered the aisle but "forgot it was there" at the moment she tripped over it.

Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint by submitting evidence demonstrating that the cart stacked with empty boxes "was open and obvious, as it was not only readily observable by those employing the reasonable use of their senses, but was known to the plaintiff prior to the accident, and, as a matter of law, was not inherently dangerous" ( Ramirez v Creative Linen House, Inc. , 170 AD3d 913 , 913 [2019]; see Flaim v Hex Food, Inc. , 79 AD3d 797 , 798 [2010]). In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Contrary to the [*2] plaintiff's contention, under the circumstances here, the condition was not a trap for the unwary ( see Gleyzer v SNL Meat & Produce, Inc. , 135 AD3d 817 , 818 [2016]; Russo v Home Goods, Inc. , 119 AD3d at 925). The cart in the aisle was readily observable by those making a reasonable use of their senses, and the plaintiff acknowledged in her affidavit that she observed the cart when she entered the aisle but "forgot it was there" at the moment she tripped over it.

The plaintiff failed to demonstrate that summary judgment was premature as she did not "offer[ ] an[y] evidentiary basis to suggest that additional discovery may lead to relevant evidence, or that facts essential to opposing the motion were exclusively within the knowledge and control of [the defendant]" ( Brooklyn Cancer Care Med., P.C. v Brooklyn Hosp. Ctr. , 201 AD3d 861 , 862 [2022]).
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

However, "there is no duty to protect or warn against an open and obvious condition that, as a matter of law, is not inherently dangerous" ( Lebron v City of New York , 208 AD3d 656 , 657 [2022] [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Cupo v Karfunkel , 1 AD3d 48 , 52 [2003]).

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the September 6, 2018 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice on defendants’ exterior stairs on January 25, 2016. An awning covered the landing and part of the steps; plaintiffs attributed the ice to melting and refreezing snow from that awning.

legal_issues.finding: Actual knowledge of the recurring condition underlies the notice analysis; no separate finding of actual notice of this particular ice patch was made.
The court applied the rule imputing notice of recurrence when a specific recurrent danger is actually known; defendants failed their initial recurrence/notice burden.
Defendants failed to negate a recurring melting-snow condition and notice. The court did not conclusively find recurrence or notice.
An unidentified remaining defense contention was not properly before the court; the basis was not specified.

quality.notes: Owned premises and stairs support private status. Preserve the source’s awkward double-negative notice wording as a burden failure, not absence or conclusive proof of recurrence. No evidence format, use, role or storm finding inferred; generic noncreation burden is not a separate creation holding.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On January 25, 2016, the plaintiff Anthony D'Amato (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on ice on the steps of an exterior stairway at premises owned by the defendants. An awning covered the stairway landing and part of the steps.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Debra Silber, J.), dated September 6, 2018. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Specifically, they alleged that the injured plaintiff's fall was caused by snow on the awning melting and refreezing on the steps.

A defendant who has actual knowledge of a recurrent dangerous condition in a specific area can be charged with constructive notice of each specific reoccurrence of the condition ( see Agosto v City of New Rochelle , 114 AD3d 625 , 626 [2014]; Brown v Linden Plaza Hous. Co., Inc. , 36 AD3d 742 [2007]). The defendants failed to meet their burden of establishing, prima facie, that snow melting from the top of the awning onto the stairs was not a recurring condition of which they did not have notice.

Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny their motion without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiffs' opposition papers ( see Winegrad v New York Univ. Med. Ctr. , 64 NY2d 851, 853 [1985]).
The defendants' remaining contention is not properly before us.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the October 18, 2017 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on water in the vestibule of defendant’s building. The time she and her friend took to return from the store was unclear, leaving the duration of the water unresolved.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant did not establish that the assistant followed the cleaning schedule or when inspection last occurred. Unclear return timing left the water’s duration unresolved; plaintiff’s burden never shifted.

evidence_discussed.description: Superintendent’s account omitted adherence to the janitorial schedule and last inspection. The opinion uses testify or aver without specifying the submission format.
Deposition did not clarify plaintiff/friend’s return timing; deponent is not identified.

quality.notes: Review private status: generic defendant’s building and janitorial staff do not expressly establish private ownership/control rather than management of unspecified premises. Management name alone is insufficient. Vestibule is entrance; no residential use, tenancy/date or maintenance records inferred.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Barbara Jaffe, J.), entered October 18, 2017, which denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
in this action where plaintiff slipped and fell on water in the vestibule of defendant's building.

Defendant failed to make a prima facie showing that it lacked constructive notice because the superintendent failed to testify or aver that his assistant adhered to a janitorial schedule on the day of the accident or when the area was last inspected prior to plaintiff's fall

Defendant also failed to establish that it lacked constructive notice on the basis that the water was not present in the vestibule for a sufficient period to afford defendant an opportunity to discover and remedy the condition

Whether the water was present for that sufficient period presents an outstanding factual issue, as the time it took plaintiff and her friend to return to the premises from the store is unclear, and defendant failed to clarify the issue at the deposition.
